Would the minister indicate just what activities will be housed in this armoury and what justification there is for such an enormous expenditure in Vancouver at this time?

Supply-National Defence-Relief Works

Of course that immediately raises a question of policy. This armoury was decided upon a year ago, and in my opinion is one of the most necessary in the Dominion, of Canada. I have not seen the armoury since it has been completed but I am informed that it is one of the most beautiful buildings in Canada, and the citizens of Vancouver are exceedingly proud of the building as such. Strictly speaking these armouries are not supposed to be used for ordinary purposes, but that rule is relaxed very frequently. Only the other day in the city of Vancouver we were able to have the armoury used for a tremendous motor show, which drew thousands upon thousands of the citizens of Vancouver for five or six days, thereby adding quite substantially to the communal pride of that city. I think these strict regulations could be relaxed very successfully in many cases, to make them available for communal purposes and so on.
In regard to the necessity for armouries, of course that is entirely a question of policy. But as long as we have defence forces in Canada; as long as we are concerned with the essential problem of national security, we must have armouries. My own judgment is that as far as possible we should endeavour to combine the essential purpose of armouries with communal enterprise and have these buildings used for other purposes to a certain extent.

Did I understand the minister to say that this armoury will be available for all community endeavours in addition to those he has mentioned? If my recollection serves me aright, when an armoury is requested for charitable purposes or for the use of service organizations of the city usually the association of officers commanding is very reluctant to give consent, complaining that the activities of the militia are interfered with. From my knowledge of the activities of the militia in Vancouver I do not think they are so great as to warrant any reluctance in giving consent in such cases.

My hon. friend is quite correct, that all this must be subject to the necessities of militia training, because the primary function of an armoury is to permit the militia to carry on their training, whatever it may be. As far as possible, however, with the consent of the district officer commanding, they might be used for other purposes, subject to certain conditions.
I just want to ask the minister what part of this $19,43325 is unexpended.
It is all committed and I think by now it is practically all payable.

Then what are we voting it for? The payments have been made as the work has progressed, under the statute of last year. The auditor general cannot pay under this statute that has not been passed, but payments are being made from day to day.
This is the unpaid balance due and owing to the contractors, Smith Bros, and Wilson, on this particular armoury.
But part of these payments have been made since these estimates were brought in, in one case at least. I do not know whether that is so in this case.
Not in this case.

I desire to ask the minister if he would indicate exactly what form of training is carried on in this armoury. Is it confined strictly to military training or is any attention given to the physical development of youth?
No, I think not; I think the training is confined entirely to the militia training as laid down, combined with lectures by company officers and the ordinary processes of militia training.

Well, I am glad to be out of order, because otherwise we would not be noticed. I shall try to abide by your decision, sir, and I hope that in the next estimate there will be an appropriate amount for the citizens of my district.

The minister I hope will bear with me in questioning this item. Request has been made frequently for funds to be appropriated for other purposes. The minister may take pride in the construction of this armoury, but he will agree that it is impossible to take pride in the housing conditions in the same area. In my opinion the money would be much better spent on the improvement of housing conditions. I do not see that the activities for which facilities are provided in this building justify the expenditure. I urge the minister for the benefit of hon. members of the committee, to make at this point a frank statement in regard to the policy of his department. A former minister of defence, under whose auspices the project was commenced, stated that these preparations were necessary not so much for national defence as to deal with the possibility of civil disturbance. Disquieting rumours in this regard have been spreading in Vancouver, and I would like some statement from the minister as to the preparations in regard to the possibility of civil disturbance.

I think that question could with more propriety be raised on the general estimates than on these special supplementaries. But I would say at once with reference to the question asked that the policy of the Department of National Defence is concerned with the national security of the Dominion of Canada.

The minister may expect the same criticism as was voiced in this house last year. Armouries are necessary in Canada. In the large cities the militia cannot much longer stand things as they are. Officers, non-commissioned officers and men get no pay; they provide funds out of their own pockets for equipment and so forth to operate their unit. They get very little of the money that they used to get under the Militia Act. Since I have been in the house the estimates of this department have come down from $24,000,000 to $13,000,000. This is a revote. The unit concerned is a splendid unit which had a fine record in the war. It was the armed strength of the barons that made magna oharta possible, and the same principle holds to-day; the disarmament of the free is the tyrant's opportunity, as we have seen in Ethiopia. We shall have a rude awakening in this country some day. We are dependent on the motherland, the permanent militia is run down, the militia in general run down, the camps are going to pieces, the cadet movement has been destroyed. We would not have been able to take the position we did in 1914 but for the cadet movement. Let me say to the hon. member who spoke before the hon. member for Vancouver North that no province owes more bo the protection of the British fleet than the province of Quebec. These armouries are necessary at the present time not only in Vancouver but in every province. Owing to the depression the department has not been able to support the militia. These men in the Seaforth battalion give their services for nothing; many of them are returned men, and they are just as fond of peace and security and just as much opposed to war as are the hon. gentlemen who are opposing this vote, for whom they fought on land and sea and in the air in the last war. They are opposed to war because they were overseas and know what war is, as those of us who stayed at home do not. Yesterday the minister was a hero; he was one of the few that could take it. Yesterdhy he was a thing of beauty and a joy forever, but to-day it is different; this is wash day.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Shall the item carry?

This item and other items of the same kind, I should say to the hon. member for Vancouver North, were included in the public works bills of 1934 and 1936 for two reasons; first, because they were necessary works; second, because they were works that afforded a maximum of a certain type of employment. In all these the proportion of

Supply-National Defence-Relief Works
material and labour was very great. They were scattered over every part of the country.
As far as the Seaforth Highlanders are concerned, I have only this to say: that that armoury had to be built if the unit was to be maintained. The unit has a record of which this country has been justifiably proud. The officers who give their time to this and other units of the kind are spending their own money, whether they be honorary officers or otherwise, and finding themselves at the end of the year much poorer than at the beginning. It must not be forgotten that the foundation of our national effort in this country in 1914 was the militia. These men, these young citizen soldiers, if you call them that, are assuming, by the very terms of their enlistment, the possibility of losing their lives in the defence of law and order in this country. They may be called to do such police duties as are provided for by the act. Surely the country is not so lacking in gratitude to men who thus offer their services for the preservation of our institutions as not to provide them with decent quarters in which to train and make a home for their unit. But the primary object that brought into being these items was the necessity for providing employment, and while so doing completing useful and necessary structures. We spent I believe several weeks on the second branch of that discussion in the years 1934 and 1935, and I think it is only fair to say that the house by a very large majority, including many of those who sat to the left of the Speaker, were satisfied that these were works that afforded a substantial amount of direct employment and an expenditure for material that gave employment in factories and various other industrial undertakings throughout Canada and local work on a large scale. Hon. members were satisfied that these works were a present and urgent necessity if we are to maintain the efficiency and effectiveness of our units of voluntary citizen soldiers that we call our militia. That is the story.

I think the minister was quite right when he intimated that matters of policy should be discussed on the main estimates rather than on these supple-mentaries. But since certain remarks have been made by various hon. members, those of us who are in a minority in this house in holding different views can hardly let those remarks pass without at least a word of comment.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) has just suggested that those whom he calls these young citizen soldiers who are willing to lay down their lives in police duty are the people who are defending and maintaining
the institutions of this country. I dissent decidedly from that point of view. The people who are maintaining the institutions of this country ane the ordinary people of the country who are carrying on, living decent lives and trying to provide for the maintenance of our community affairs. If the institutions of this country fail it will be because those in charge of them have failed in their duty of providing for the common people. I do not think there is any section of Canada that holds anarchistic ideas or that wants to tear down, but I do assert that there are limits beyond which no free people can be driven. As we have stated so often, when we have over a million people on relief and large numbers of people who continue to be unemployed year after year,, until they become almost desperate and occasionally break out in rioting, I say it is the people who are neglecting to provide work and opportunity who are responsible for any fracas that may occasionally break out.
If we are going to maintain our institutions we shall do so by carrying out the principles for which our institutions should stand. If we are going to depend upon the police to maintain our institutions, a rather popular doctrine to-day I am afraid, then we may as well abandon these institutions. We are a free people. Our forefathers adopted these institutions because through them they expressed their community and national life. In the old days they did not think it necessary to have a group of hirelings, a group of mercenaries to maintain our institutions. Each stood ready to defend our institutions in the very best- way, namely by using them to advantage. I regret exceedingly that we have lapsed so easily into the idea that our national institutions have to be defended by force.
I shall not discuss the matter in further detail, but shall make only one or two observations on the point mentioned by the leader of the opposition, that these operations were begun because it was considered they would supply a very considerable amount of work for the unemployed. At the time the suggestion was made, some of us protested against this type of project. In the first place, if we are to have public works, in the old sense in which the term is used, that is public buildings devoted to public service, there are other types that are needed more than barracks. We need places where the great masses of our people in our communities can come together for various community enterprises.
In this city of Ottawa there is one building that is denounced as a disgrace; I refer to

Supply-National Defence-Relief Works
the supreme court building. I should fancy that a dignified home for the Supreme Court of Canada would be more desirable than a great number of barracks erected across the country. That is one suggestion, if we are to have public buildings.
But most of us would go farther than that and say that under conditions existing to-day we do not need public buildings as much as another type of building, namely homes for our people. In my home city of Winnipeg one of these huge public buildings has been erected. Well, it is a fine building; I do not object to it as a building, but I do know a great many owners of private office buildings were not very glad when the new federal building was erected. I know, further, that according to the housing report of the city of Winnipeg there are most abominable housing conditions almost within the shadow of that big federal building. The point I should like to emphasize is that the building of houses for the people would provide just as much work and probably more than would the erection of a building such as the one under discussion. I believe the building of homes would give more work, because a smaller amount of the work is done by machinery used so extensively by contractors on big structures. The building of homes would provide work and at the same time it would provide in large sections of our community a very real and vital need.
A difficulty arises because of the way in which we handle the estimates. They are brought forward and we are asked either to accept or to criticize them. We cannot reject them, but we can criticize them. But there is no way in which we can balance one kind of enterprise against another kind. I may be in favour of this particular kind of building; possibly I should not like to vote it down, in so far as it may provide a certain amount of work. But the only thing we can do is to criticize it as severely as we can, knowing that there are many other works much more vital to the welfare of the community which could be entered upon. The performance of those other works would accomplish the end of providing employment. That is one difficulty in this haphazard departmentalized way of introducing the government's program. We have not any general review of the whole situation.
I should not have made these remarks at this time but would have reserved them until later had it not been that I feel I must protest against the opinion so generally and freely expressed by some people that we must maintain a military establishment.

By the way, the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church) referred rather slightingly to some of us who remained at home during the last war. I am not a bit ashamed of having remained at home in the last war, although I like a great many others was not in the eligible class. I am not ashamed that I did not go to the front; that is one of the things of which I feel proud. But may I say that in his slighting remarks the hon. member for Broadview included the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil).
No, he did not.
I thought that was done.
No.

All I wish to say in passing is that if there is any virtue in having gone to war and having been among the most distinguished there, then my colleague from Vancouver North has that advantage. In the development of our country we have reached the stage where, whether we went to war or stayed at home, we ought surely to be able to express ourselves on matters of national defence without having any slurs cast upon us. Some of us feel that in opposing these military defence estimates we are just as patriotic as any hon. members who propose them. We look at things from a different angle, but as hon. members of the house we think we ought to be in a position frankly to state our position with regard to matters, without being subjected to slurs from any part of the house.

In questioning the expenditure I did not intend to cast any slur on the record of the Seaforth Highlanders. I know the record of that regiment, and would not wittingly east any reflection upon its record or glorious traditions. But may I point out that the men who to-day form the Seaforth Highlanders of Vancouver are not the men who gained glory and distinction for that regiment from 1914 to 1918. I cannot let the occasion pass without reminding hon. members that many of the former members of the Seaforth Highlanders, a regiment which gained glory and distinction on the field of battle, are to-day begging bread in and around the city of Vancouver. We should not overlook that fact.
I rather regret the suggestion that the regiment is now being maintained and housed in the manner suggested strictly for police duty. I cannot believe-

No one said that.

No, that has not been suggested.

matter.

I am glad to hear that
correction. I shonld not like to have the suggestion go out that the regiment would be standing to, as it were, waiting for some civil disturbances.
No.

I wish to make it clear
that I question our readiness to spend money in such large sums merely for the purpose of policing our country when those expenditures should be counterbalanced by even greater expenditures designed to remove the causes of discontent which may lead to disorder. The point I wish to make clear is that it is vastly more important to prevent disorder than to suppress it once an outbreak has occurred.

I do not know that there is very much I can say about this except to draw attention to the fact that this country has reached a very inglorious position when its defences have to be carried out on a sustenance basis of food, clothing, shelter and twenty cents per day to the labour employed. It is only fair to say that the steel and other technical work was done by men who were paid regular wages. There was a camp there and work had to be provided for the men, if only for exercise purposes. If any of the men in the camp could get a job, they were free to take it. There is, of course, no comparison between the funded debt of a company and its securities, issued under the Philadelphia plan or otherwise. Page 28 of the Canadian National Railways report for 1935 makes that quite clear. Issues that sell at 112 are the funded debt of the corporation. Its equipment trust certificates, which are serials, are dealt with, not on the basis of a yield or payment of so much interest but on the basis of how much per $100 they will realize. They do it the converse way. We say interest at 44 per cent, so and so; they say it is to yield such and such a rate, and it is the rate yield which they pay and on which the certificates are bought and sold on

the market. So far as 4J per cent and other rates charged are concerned, these were the rates negotiated by the companies themselves without reference to the government, because the security for the loan was the equipment. The government does not guarantee. The security is the equipment itself, and on each piece of equipment there is a metal strip indicating that the particular piece of equipment is the property of the trust company, that is to say, the trustee under the arrangement under -which the equipment is bought. So far as the 4 per cent rate is concerned, it is a lower rate than the railway negotiated for any of its securities prior to 1930. In 1930 the last negotiation for equipment made by the Canadian National was the L series, 4J per cent, the date of issue being June 1, 1930, and date of maturity June 1, 1945, and the principal outstanding December 31, 1935, was $10,500,000, the interest being $492,187.50. The lessening of the interest for two years meant, of course, two years' interest on the entire $15,000,000, because the serials did not begin to be paid until the transaction was completed. Then they would have free interest for two years; and that, of course, reduced the rate below 4 per cent, a lower rate than they could secure on their own if they went on the market. Neither of our railways was able to sell equipment trust securities. The Canadian Pacific Railway is registered under the Securities Act, but the Canadian National is not, or was not until recently, although before the late government went out of office the dominion government did register under the provisions of that act. They were not so anxious about getting the equipment as we were to afford employment, which was the primary purpose for which this action was taken. The primary purpose behind this effort was to
give employment to a class of men who were and had been idle for years, except for such work as they had obtained in consequence of government orders in Hamilton, in Montreal, in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, and possibly in some other town, as well as in the shops at Point St. Charles and one of the western shops and the shops at Angus, Montreal. That was the purpose of this arrangement and it is limited to $15,000,000. Seven million dollars.
- Mr. BENNETT: And the Canadian National eight million dollars. The arrangement was made after a good deal of negotiation and the rate fixed, having regard to the period of time for which no interest was paid, was regarded as very fair.

I should not like to leave the impression that I am criticizing the item. I am entirely in favour of the action taken, of making a loan of $15,000,000; I think it is perfectly sound. I still press this point, however, that where we are making loans to railways or anywhere else it is desirable to get the interest rates down to the lowest possible level, because this will have an influence on the general rate of interest. I know there are two schools of thought on the question of lowering interest rates, but I am deeply impressed with the effect of the burden of debt, whether public or corporate or private. So great is it that we must take every possible means and seize every opportunity to reduce that burden, and the best way in which we can do so if we desire to escape some form of repudiation is to reduce the rate of interest. I have never at any time, in my arguments on financial matters, given countenance to the suggestion of repudiation, but I cannot escape the conviction that we must not overlook any opportunity of beating down the rates of interest on any of these new issues. In regard to these matters, in connection with the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National, if we loan them money we should try to secure the lowest rate possible, in the hope that this will have an influence on the general rate of interest for commerce and industry throughout the country as a whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Fisheries) :
speechtext:
When this bill was last before the
house I was trying to explain, when the hour for private bills expired, the purpose of the act and the reasons for the regulations complained of by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). That purpose is to prohibit by statutory enactment fishing with seine boats in a certain area at the mouth of the Fraser river in the bay of Georgia. Under the Fisheries Act the governor in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Fisheries, may approve regulations permitting such fishing in that area. This bill is to prevent such permission being given either by order in council or by the Minister of Fisheries.
The regulation authorizing this mode of fishing came into force in 1933, the year following the adoption by order in council of regulations with regard to the inspection of canned salmon on the British Columbia coast. It has been alleged that these regulations for the sanctioning by order in council of this mode of fishing were passed for the purpose of favouring a particular class, namely, the canners. As I have already said, I cannot judge the motives which inspired those who were responsible for the legislation, but I said and I repeat now that I cannot believe they were actuated by such motives. It seems that the regulation permitting this manner of fishing in the area in question was passed solely for the purpose of assisting a class of fishermen who otherwise would not have derived any great benefit from the catch of the late run of salmon in these

Fisheries Act-Mr. Michaud
waters towards the end of September and in October every odd year. That is the late run of sockeye salmon in the fall.
It is admitted by some, at least, that during the late summer, the end of August and the early fall in every odd year, there is a class of fish which come up the Fraser river for the purpose of spawning along the upper regions of that river, and before they reach the mouth of the river, while they are still in sea water, they are in such a condition that they can be caught and properly packed, provided they are properly graded later. The Americans, who are permitted to fish with seines and seine boats up to the imaginary boundary line in the gulf of Georgia, derive great profits from that mode of fishing, and if it were thought advisable to allow our Canadian fishermen to derive the same benefit, obvious advantages would result. A certain area has been mapped out and is well known to those familiar with conditions on the coast, and since 1933, on two occasions, as I am informed, fishermen of that region derived monetary benefits from large hauls of that fish, which, when caught with seines in the cold salt water, were packed, graded mostly to standard, and put on the market, to the profit of both fishermen and canners. I could give figures as to the quantities caught, but my hon. friend the member for New Westminster put on the record the other evening certain figures which are correct and which show the value to these people of being allowed to catch that fish at that time of the year.
As I said before, this regulation was passed and made it possible, in view of previous regulations of the year 1932, to inspect the fish when packed, and it was possible to detect in some degree whether the fish caught in the fall was then in marketable condition.
The privileges set forth in this regulation can be availed of only in every other year. This year, I understand, there will be no fall run of pink or sockeye, so the regulation will have no application in 1936.
That is a fact, is it?
That is what is reported by the officers of the department. In making that statement I rely on their report.
Quite so.

I believe that all the salmon caught either with seine or with gill nets at that period of the year is Canada first grade or extra good quality. From information available to the department it seems that it is only the fish caught in cold, 12739-160i
salt or sea water that comes up to grade 1 or grade A or Canada first, as it may be called, and can go on the market as such. The 'house will readily understand that it is of great benefit to the fishermen to obtain the fish in that condition, because if they do not catch it with seines it gets into warmer water, where it can be caught with gill nets, but it is not as firm, as hard, or as good as when caught right in the sea. Further, under those circumstances our fishermen are not on the same footing or enjoying the same advantages as are the American fishermen, who are privileged to catch the fish while it is in colder and salter water.
It is possible that the area over which these people are permitted to fish with seines is too large, and that over part of it the gill netters could catch the same quantity of fish. If it is found that this regulation is detrimental tc the interests of some class of people on the coast there is no question but that it will be. revised. But before doing so, I submit, the department will need a more careful investigation of local conditions. It is possible that for the year 1937 the extent of the area to be reduced could be limited only to that part of the water at the mouth of the Fraser river and in the gulf of Georgia which extends between the boundary line across the gulf and, say to Lulu island on one side, and to Galiano or to Valdes island on the other. In this way we could reduce by about fifty per cent the area, limiting it only to that area which is covered by clear, cold, salt sea water, limiting it to the area close to the boundary line where our competitors can avail themselves of a privilege which we are trying to deny to our British Columbia fishermen. If the house think that they should enjoin the minister or the governor in council to prohibit by law this mode of fishing, I submit that, from all the information which is before us, we do not think this would be in the best interests of the fishermen themselves. It might enable them to catch the same quantity of fish in the fall, but it would certainly not enable them to catch the fish in as good a condition as they can do by means of seines further down in the gulf, and so would deprive them of the privilege of competing with American fishermen just across the line.
I can assure the house that these regulations are not continued or enforced with a view of hurting any class or unduly benefiting any other class of persons interested in the fisheries of British Columbia. As far as the department is concerned the fishermen have to be protected. I believe that the interests of the canners are just as much the interests of the gill net fishermen as of the seine net fishermen.
Fisheries Act-Mr. Michaud

After all, if the fish is not good and in first class condition the canners will not pay the highest price for it; they may not can it, or if they do it will be classified, on inspection, as grade 2 salmon, of a lower quality. Thus, I believe, the interests of those whom we are trying to protect by this legislation would be injuriously affected.
I submit to my hon. friend that before revoking the power which has been given and before prohibiting this mode of fishing, we should give some consideration to the effect this would have on our trade, as well as to the effect on the fishermen themselves. It may be that if they were not allowed to catch that special class of salmon with gill nets, we would have either to prohibit the late fishing of salmon, as was the case years ago, or to make more stringent regulations regarding inspection, and brand as inferior salmon caught at the mouth of the Fraser river. I submit that either of these alternatives would be more injurious to those fishermen than to regulate their mode of fishing, even though some of them are not privileged to catch as much as are the others. Therefore I submit that my hon. friend should wait another year before seeking to repeal this regulation. In the meantime the department will 1-ook into the matter; we will make a special study of conditions, and if we find that for the protection of the industry it is necessary to do away with this regulation we certainly will repeal it without hesitation.

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I must say to my hon. friend sponsoring this bill (Mr. Reid) that I do not see my way clear to support the measure at this time. Knowing as I do how earnest he is in his views on this matter, this adds to my regret, and I may say if I felt that his apprehensions with regard to the injury to the gill net fishermen were well founded I certainly would support him. However I think he is perhaps unduly alarmed in that respect and their interests will not be affected nearly as seriously as he apprehends. Indeed, I question if they will be affected at all, if the seining operations are kept at a reasonable distance away from the mouth of the river.
Let me indicate why I believe that to be true. It is of course known to all, and it should be remembered, that at one time the Fraser river was one of the most marvellous salmon rivers in the world. I can recall that when I first went to British Columbia, now forty-two years ago, the run of salmon up the Fraser was such that if one were to tell what one had seen he would be branded as

the champion liar of the fishing season. So I shall not risk my reputation by indicating what I have actually seen, not only at the mouth of the Fraser river but hundreds of miles up in the interior, on the tributaries of that great river. It will be recalled also, however, that one of the most severe blows to fishing on the Fraser river was occasioned by the construction of the Canadian Northern railway, as it was then called. While this work was proceeding down the Fraser canyon the side of a mountain was blasted out, and a huge quantity of rock fell into the river, literally blocking the gorge in such a manner that salmon were very seriously impeded; in fact it threatened the extinction of salmon fishing on the Fraser river. Then, at considerable cost-I think almost wholly to the government, though part of it may have been borne by the railway-steps were taken, in order to give the fish freer passage, to remove this slide or to minimize the damage that had been done. Since then, fishing on the Fraser river has substantially improved, though of course it is still pitifully low in comparison with what it used to be.
Another point to be borne in mind is this: The salmon runs that come up the Fraser very largely enter

I am not going to be dogmatic about this-through the strait of Juan de Fuca,' come up through the gulf of Georgia and strike the mainland coast below the boundary, on the Washington side. Then they come up the coast and go up the Skagit and other smaller rivers emptying into the gulf, and into the mouth of the Fraser, and of course some of them go further up. Along through that area there are quite extensive shallows, and the fish like to hover round th-ose shallows for a few days before proceeding up the river. That, I think, is the habit of the salmon as far as that is concerned.
For many years the Americans have allowed fishing out in the gulf with those great purse seines described by the hon. member for New Westminster the other evening. These very numerous vessels of United States registry would go into the gulf and, as indicated the other night, sight the schools of fish coming in and catch very large quantities of them. On the Canadian side we did not allow seining. For many years this question has been before each succeeding government, but seining was not allowed until very recently, within the last couple of years; I have forgotten the exact date. I see no reason at all why we should not permit purse seine fishing on the Canadian side providing it is kept at a considerable distance from the mouth of the Fraser river.

Fisheries Act-Mr. Stevens
I hope the minister will uccept what I have to say in a kindly way if I differ with him on one or two minor points, because it is not reasonable to expect him to be completely familiar with all the details, and particularly with the geography of the country. The minister mentioned that if the area were restricted by a line drawn from Lulu island across to Galiano island, and so on, it would keep purse seines far enough back. I submit, however, that this would not be the case, because Lulu island is the delta of the Fraser river. One arm of the river runs out to the north and the other main arm runs to the south. Certainly I believe purse seine fishing should be kept beyond some point very much further out than that. I would suggest that the line should be drawn three, four or possibly five miles out, because the flats or shallows run out for a considerable distance, and no purse seine fishing should be allowed there.
My hon. friend in his bill has indicated a certain area, running I think directly west from Point Grey-he will correct me if I am not describing this correctly-to the northern end of Galiano island and thence southwesterly, I suppose, to the international boundary, the outer range light, which, I assume, is the one on the westerly side of the gulf of Georgia where it intersects the international boundary on the westerly side of the gulf, thence back to the point of commencement. The area so described means taking in the whole of the gulf between the islands on the west and the mainland south of that line. So, instead of that, I suggest -that if purse seine fishing were prohibited within a certain distance, say five miles, of the mainland and the Lulu island shore line at the mouth of the Fraser, and permitted out in the gulf beyond that, I do not think any injury would be done to the gill net fishermen. The gill net fishermen fish largely in and off the mouth of the Fraser, over the sand shallows along the coast and up the river. I do not think there is much gill net fishing far out in the gulf, so that I see no particular damage to be done to the gill net fishermen if purse seine fishing were limited in that way.
I regret the frequent attacks which are made upon the officers of the Department of Fisheries. We may differ in opinion regarding the policy followed by the department; I see ample room for that, but it is unfortunate that officers of the department should be in a sense held responsible for the policies adopted. It is true that these officials advise the minister, but I would remind hon. members who are prone to be bitterly critical of them, that we members of parliament have ample opportunity to present any views we
may hold which conflict with those advanced by officers of the department. It is a mistake publicly to denounce these officials, because during the twenty-five years that I have been in parliament-and I think some of them have been in the department during almost that whole period-I have always found them extremely careful men who used their best judgment. I have heard it stated that they are unduly influenced by the canning interests, but I do not think that is the case. I cannot recall in my memory of the record of the department that these officials have been unduly influenced by the canners. I know that the canners have frequently advanced views which were peculiarly in their own interests and which conflicted with those of the fishermen. That, of course, is to be expected, but I believe that the department generally, speaking through its permanent officials, has been reasonably impartial in that respect. I know there are hon. members who will differ perhaps sharply from this statement, but that is my view based upon considerable experience with the department. So I believe, not that the officials are infallible, but that their advice might very well be followed in this matter, particularly in view of the fact that the fishing is of a kind which will not seriously compete with or affect the gill net fishermen.
There is another point, which again I think is a question of fact. It has been stated positively that fish caught in the purse seines are damaged; I think some claim that they become smothered in the mass that naturally is drawn together when the seine is pursed and ready for lifting. I do not profess to have expert knowledge, but I have some familiarity with the matter and my impression is just the contrary. There might occasionally be an unusually heavy purse and some fish damaged; I think that is without doubt, but on the whole I believe that the fish caught in the purse seines would be in just as good or better condition than those caught in the gill nets, particularly if the latter were caught any distance up the river.
At this point I would like to differ in a very kindly way with the minister in his reference to the condition of fish as they are caught in the gill nets and in the purse seines. He said that there was a very great advantage in having the fish caught in clear water. There is a measure of truth in that, but I think the minister over-emphasized the point, because when the salmon come into the brackish waters, the fresh waters flowing out of the mouth of the Fraser, which by the way turn largely down the coasf^-you can easily see the line of demarcation some miles
Fisheries Act-Mr. Barber

out from the shore-the water, changed somewhat by the tide, turns southward and the salmon hover in that area. I do not think a particle of damage is done to the salmon while they are there. In fact some hold the view that the salmon improve in condition while in that area, not if they remain there long, but I believe it is not their habit to remain there very long. So I do not attach much weight to the suggestion that the fish caught in the gill nets in the mouth of the Fraser are in any sense deteriorated by their stay in that area.
Then there is the question of inspection. Here, again, I know that certain hon. members will differ sharply in opinion with me, and I respect the sincerity of their views; yet I am bound to say that careful consideration has convinced me that the system of inspection has been definitely and distinctly beneficial to Canadian interests. I had some experience in connection with exports from Canada and external trade matters, and an opportunity of discussing the subject from many angles with disinterested persons, and I am convinced that inspection is desirable and the need of it imperative. I am not saying that the present scheme of inspection is perfect, but I say that it is a very good one and I certainly do not agree with the denunciation of it that I have heard. When a certain part of a pack is discovered to be not No. 1 but grade No. 2, or some other grade, the department placed in its regulations an order that a second lid should be put on, which second lid would be stamped with the second grade mark, so as clearly to indicate it.
Then it was charged that certain exporters or those who were handling the export business, would remove that second lid and leave the can in its original condition, namely showing the No. 1 mark. Of course that is most reprehensible, and any one found to have done this should certainly be punished. It is fraud of the rankest bind, and should not be allowed under any circumstances. The minister and his department should and, I believe, could devise some method which would overcome the difficulty. I have no doubt that the question has been already considered and I hope measures have been provided to deal with it.
I wish to register definite approval of the general system of inspection, which I hope will be continued and maintained. If it can be improved or strengthened I certainly would approve any such action. Perhaps I had better put it in this way: I would urge the minister not to give way in any sense

by removing or abandoning the system of inspection or, I will put it in this way, "a" system of inspection, because I believe that inspection such as was inaugurated a few years ago is decidedly to the benefit of the export business in salmon. We must remember that a great deal of this is export business, and it is most desirable that the high standard of our salmon should be maintained.
Perhaps I might as well say, in passing, that there are many varieties of salmon packed for export and for sale, and it may well be that the department could take into consideration a clearer distinction between the different grades or types of salmon placed on the market. Sometimes there is a tendency to use a name which would indicate that the article was British Columbia salmon. While the label might not indicate that it was sockeye, it would convey the impression that it was No. 1 salmon when, as a matter of fact, it might be a very poor pink, a humpback, a cohoe or some other distinctly inferior brand. That part of the business should be carefully guarded. The high standard of British Columbia sockeye should be maintained in its integrity, at all costs.
I believe I have nothing further to say. I say to the hon. member most earnestly that I do not see my way clear to support his bill. I believe he would be well advised to accept the suggestion of the minister, let it rest for another year and give it still further consideration and study. I want him to know I am sympathetic towards the interests of his constituents, the fishermen, because they, along with other fishermen in other parts of the country, have certainly had a hard enough time. However I do not think this bill would be of any distinct advantage or help to them. It is for these reasons that I cannot support the hon. member's bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to congratulate the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) upon the moderation with which as a layman he presented his case. It was admirably presented in every way, and had he not devoted his life to acquiring skill with the bagpipes he certainly would have been an admirable legal practitioner.
I rise for only one purpose. If the statements made by the hon. member regarding the frauds practised by those who can salmon are accurate, then immediate action should be taken. That a double can should be prepared and that the methods indicated by the hon. member should be followed is a sad reflection upon this country. I stress the hope that the minister will take immediate steps to see to it that there will be no repetition of the frauds practised upon the purchasing public if-and
I put the word "if" in large letters-the facts as stated by the hon. member are correct. I am sure he stated them as he believed them, but it is difficult to think that reputable manufacturers would resort to the methods indicated for the purpose of selling their product fraudulently.
So far as the general question is concerned it is, of course, competent for the minister to recommend that the order in council be rescinded. That would end the matter, without any bill. All you have to do is stay as you were. It is satisfactory to note that the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens), who at the time the order in council was passed was a representative from British Columbia in the goverenment, is still of opinion that the order in council was properly passed; because as regards the passing of that order in council we relied more or less on local knowledge. The terms in which it was enacted indicate clearly the purpose which was to be accomplished. If there are any substantial reasons why the action was not warranted, then it is always open to the government, as it was to that government, to rescind1 or to repeal the order in council. But the bill proposes to accomplish something more than that. It does not propose entirely to cancel the effect of the order in council, but to some extent to modify the field of its operation.
I have no personal views with respect to the matter and I only desire to make it perfectly clear that if the facts are as stated we should not hesitate for a minute to take every possible action to prevent the continuation of such frauds upon the purchasing public.
With respect to the other matter it is always open for the government of my right hon. friend with its vast majority, to which my hon. friend sometimes refers, to accomplish his purpose without having any reference whatever to a bill in parliament, presumably like General Parkinson's reference to Disraeli, who had a resolution in his pocket but would proceed by bill if advisable. It is competent to rescind the order in council by order in council, rather than proceed by a bill.

Mr. Speaker, the few minutes left before nine o'clock will not allow me to deal with all the arguments that have been advanced this evening. At the outset let me say that I appreciate very much the kind words of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett),, and I can assure him in regard to his remarks about me that if I were as good a lawyer as I am a player, I would be some lawyer.
Fisheries Act-Mr. Reid

I also appreciate the fact that the minister who is in charge of the Fisheries department (Mr. Michaud) does not know the district in question as those of us from British Columbia do, but I am pleased that he is going to go out there to look over the situation for himself, and I was glad to hear his statement that if it is found that a wrong has been done to the gill net fishermen, the regulations will be changed. I realize that close to the international boundary there is clear water, but the greater part of the area has been fished by gill net fishermen since confederation.
The hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) referred to my attack on the officials of the department. It is true that in the House of Commons I personally have criticized the officials, but I have done so only after coming to the conclusion that their attitude was against the fishermen; at least, that is my belief. I shall give only one instance, and that is in connection with the embargo which had existed from confederation against the export of sockeye salmon from the Fraser river to the United States. When we urged in this house, and were supported by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), that the embargo should be lifted and the fishermen allowed to sell their fish in the highest market, the officials said: If that happens, Gabriel might as well blow his trumpet, for all is over with the fishermen. Every time we advocated this they said that it should not be done, and that it would be just too bad for the fishing industry if it were done. Well, it was done last year and nothing serious has happened. The fisherman is still there and will be for a long time. The cannery men are still operating there even though the fishermen are allowed to ship their fish, and nothing that was predicted by the officials of the department has happened. That is why I am pleading with the minister and with this house to-night. The officials had not one good word to say on behalf of the gill net fishermen on the Fraser river when we discussed this matter in committee last year.
I might have asked the minister to accomplish by order in council the object sought by this bill, but realizing the stone wall of officialdom that we are up against, I felt that this was the proper place and this was the proper manner of proceeding in order to bring the matter forcibly before the new members of the House of Commons, and to get the matter remedied.
As I have pointed out, I have not the time this evening to refer to every argument

that has been made by the minister and by the hon. member for Kootenay East. The minister said that I had introduced four or five different subjects, but I would point out that most of them are related to the bilf under discussion. The treaty which Canada has signed but which has not yet been signed by the United States is related to sockeye salmon entering the Fraser river.

Signed but not ratified
by the senate.

Exactly. Now in regard to
quality, I notice that the director of fisheries in British Columbia stated publicly last year that the reason seines were allowed to fish there was in order that the fishermen might catch the fish in larger numbers. We know that to be the truth. We know that the seine boats had mobile traps and that they moved from one district to another, and they were largely owned by the canners, but that was not the reason given as in 1933. This was the last area precluded to them. The gill net fishermen had been fishing there ever since confederation, but after the seine fishing started there, the gill net fishermen were driven out, and not only that but other varieties of fish in those waters have been diminishing, for the seine boats catch almost everything within the school of fish.
I do not want to press this bill to a vote because, as stated, it does not affect the fishermen this year as the seines will not become operative in the area this year, but I think it is only right that the seine fishing industry should be given notice now that next year seine fishing will not be allowed in this area. I know that some seine fishing is necessary in open, clear water, but the district dealt with by this bill is the brackish water of the Fraser river. Under the circumstances, and looking for good results, I am perfectly willing to withdraw the bill at this time, in the hope and expectation that the minister will really look over the district for himself and not take too seriously what his officials tell him about the matter, and that seine fishing, if allowed in there at all, will be in very small proportion and confined as closely as possible to the international boundary. Believing that the minister will do something, under the circumstances, therefore, Mr. Speaker, I would ask permission to withdraw the bill.
Bill withdrawn.

Supply-Public Works-Buildings
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

['Perhaps the minister will give this item a little thought between now and next time. I have nothing more to say about it. It is opposed not because of the amount, but because of what is involved in the way of future expenditure.\nItem stands.\nProgress reported.']

This amount is to provide for carving, as requested by the chief architect of the department in a memorandum dated a few weeks ago. As the hon. gentleman and other hon. members know, there is still a large amount of carving to be done round this building. It is being done a little at a time each year, a small amount of money being placed in the estimates each year for this purpose. This will by no means complete the work, but a small amount will be undertaken this year.
For relief?

Has something been

It would occur to me, then, that this item should properly appear under the heading of "Projects already undertaken." It is not a new project at all; it is not another project but just an amount to complete a building for which provision had been made.

I am informed that this

That leads me to the

But what I have indicated was^ the reason no provision was made for the item earlier in the estimates. While the minister is

They are all Liberal anyway.

Those on relief in
Ottawa? Oh, no.
I have never met a Conservative in Ottawa outside this house.

In this vote the new expenditures are, first, Mildmay, in the constituency of Grey-Bruce; the East block in Ottawa, improvements and reconstruction

I suggest that the minister should withdraw this item of $15,000. Of course, it is not worth while talking about $15,000 here, for every item ranges from $200,000 to $1,000,000, and so on. I submit, however, that $15,000 could be saved in connection with carving in this house. Go into the lobby and look at the carving; it is spoiling good stone and is a waste of money.

I might be inclined to
agree with the hon. gentleman, but then my taste may not be good. I do not know much about the arts.

There is nothing artistic
about it. It is spoiling good stone.
Are the new projects mentioned all in Ontario or are there similar new projects elsewhere in the dominion?

There are new projects in
other sections. As far as Ontario is concerned, there are also projects covered by harbour and river developments. As regards buildings, these are the new items.
Outside the main estimates.
Certainly.

I want to ask a further question in connection with the Kingsville building. In the estimates submitted some time ago an amount of $14,500 was indicated for that building. When the original vote was introduced a year ago the amount asked for was $25,000. I assumed at the time that was to be the total cost of the Kingsville building. If you subtract the revote of $5,500 from the item of $14,500 in the main

estimates, it leaves a net amount of $9,000; and then in the estimates before us there is another $11,500, or an additional $20,500 altogether. I cannot understand how a building that was to cost $25,000 in the first place will cost now, according to my figures, $45,500. Either the building must have been doubled in size or a more expensive property must have been purchased. There must be some explanation.

The contract price for that building was $26,690. This amount of $11,500 is in addition to the amount which is included in the main estimates. The explanatory note that was given to me is that last December, at the time when the main estimates were being prepared it was anticipated that the contractor would perform work to the extent of $18,000 in the year 1935-36. Instead of that, work to the extent of $10,000 was done, leaving $8,000 to be provided. In addition to that, a clock and gable are to be installed at a cost of $1,250. The cost of fittings is increased from $3,000 to $4,500, and contingencies are increased $250, from $1,810 to $2,060.
What will be the total cost *when it is completed?
It will be $40,000. Of course, the original contract of $26,000 did not in-include the interior fittings of the building

I should like to have a clear understanding of the statement made by the minister a moment or so ago. I was astounded to learn of the procedure followed in permitting men to work in the city of Ottawa. It seems to me a very vicious principle of discrimination that men who are competent to work and desire work are not granted it unless their political beliefs are favoured by the part}' in power.
The minister did not say that at all.
I understood that a man must have a card from the Ottawa Liberal Association. However I should be glad to hear what-
That is not the case.
I understood from the words of the minister that that was the usual practice.
No, that is not the case.

Perhaps the minister will tell us what he proposes to do with the forest products building. It is a testing laboratory which, in my judgment, should be under the control of the National Research bureau. The late government declined to spend any money other than to keep up the building; I refer

Supply-P ub lie Wo rks-B uildings
to the building at Montreal. We have now no public domain on which we have forests to sell, except in the northwest territories, and we cannot sell them there. Now, that we have handed over the railway belt to British Columbia, and the natural resources to the western provinces, the provinces have complete control of all the timber in the country, but we maintain the laboratory at Montreal. It seemed to me that this was very improper, because it could be worked out with the National Research bureau, and steps were taken looking to the accomplishment of that end. To put more money into this laboratory would be, I think, wholly improper; we should have the work carried on by the institutions set up for that purpose. We are testing the tensile strength and other qualities of woods; just why, I do not know; I never was able to understand why. In view of the fact that we parted with our resources and turned them back to the provinces, and parted with the railway belt lands, we no longer have any areas of timber over which we could exercise any effective control.
The same thing comes up in connection with planting trees. The provinces now have complete control of the situation. There was a time when we had control of the whole of the northwest territories and the western provinces, but that day has long since passed. I think the minister might give some consideration as to why we are now spending money on this laboratory.
This laboratory, as my right hon. friend said, is in Montreal on the grounds of McGill university.
Exactly.

And if my information is
correct, the companies interested in our forests are contributing a certain amount of money towards the maintenance of that laboratory. At all events the Department, of Public Works, in making this grant, is only acting for another department. I, of course, have no control over this laboratory; if I am not mistaken, it is under the Department of the Interior.
That is right.

I am taking care of it only as I take care of all the public buildings for all the other departments. It is not for me to speak as to the policy involved in transferring this organization to the provincial authorities. This amount of money is for improvements only.

I know that. But the
place is about through.

Could the minister tell
the committee how these works, having particular reference to the Ottawa projects, are to be done? Will tenders be called for the various projects, with the exception of the one for the Ottawa parliament buildings? I assume that no tender will be called for that. Will tenders be called for the other items on the list having reference to Ottawa?

Yes, it is proposed to ask for tenders on all these works, when it is possible. Of course there are certain works that can be done by the ordinary employees of the departments, but, generally speaking, we shall follow' the rule and ask for tenders.

Touching on the point
which was raised by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) and was again the subject of a question by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. MacNeil), I understood the minister to say that in engaging employees for these works the usual procedure would be followed, and that to get work a person would have to have a card from a city member.
No.

If the minister did not
make that statement I wish he would make clear to the committee just what he did say, because I do not want to go away from here with a wrong impression as to w'hat he said.

What I said was this:
Nobody will complain, I suppose, if I give consideration to the representations being made by the members for Ottawa. They have the right, as 'has anybody else, to make recommendations with the view of providing work for certain people who are in need of work. That these persons may be friends of the members is no objection; members should not be prevented from recommending persons to be employed on public works because they are their friends. They have the right, like anybody else, to make recommendations. I said that we would, no doubt, take into consideration such recommendations. That has been the practice followed for years, ever since confederation, by, I suppose, all politicians. I added that as far as possible, where circumstances permitted or justified such action, any other recommendation would also be considered and the requests granted.

To me that does not
sound very convincing. I understand that this is a vote of the public moneys of Canada. Irrespective of party, the people of Canada will be taxed to raise this money, and the unemployed are not confined to supporters

of any one party. Regardless of what the practice may have been in the past, I cannot see why we should continue a practice unless it is a good one, and I doubt whether there is anybody in this house who will say that it is a good practice. They may say so when they are in office, but not when they are out of office. I believe that many of the people who voted for the Liberal party expected it to adopt new ideals, to adopt new measures, new principles and new policies, and not to follow the old practices even if they 'have been followed since confederation. See where such policies have landed us. In this city of Ottawa I have spoken to a great many unemployed, and the impression among them is that they cannot get jobs on government works unless they receive recommendations from the sitting member or someone else who is influential in the Liberal party. Whether that has been the practice or not, it seems to me that the more such a practice has prevailed, the stronger the reason why it should be abolished and we should get down to a proper basis, whereby we shall not take away the independence of our people by making it a condition that if they are to get work they must vote for a certain party.
May I be allowed to answer the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) ?
Coming events cast their shadows before.

I just want to cite my own experience, and what I am going to say I can corroborate. My experience as a member of parliament, whether the party in power was Liberal or Conservative, was that whenever work was required and undertaken for the purpose of providing employment, generally speaking the local member recommended not only those of his own party but anyone unemployed, whatever might have been his political allegiance, provided he was the head of a family and in need of work. Since the Liberal party has been in power I am sure that we have always given recommendations to those who deserved work, irrespective of their party allegiance.

The minister has entirely misstated the case. What he has said might be applicable to normal conditions, but it cannot possibly be applicable to the abnormal conditions under which these expenditures are being made. The contractors who secure the contract for the construction of a building are told-it is part of their contract in many instances, though I do not know whether or

not that is the case now-that they must give-employment to those who are really in necessitous circumstances. I will put it as broadly as that. Whenever there is an attempt to-interfere with the contractor, in connection with relief undertakings I think the minister should be adamant in preventing that being, done. It is a terrible thing; I say it is terrible because I saw evidences of it in one case. It is distressing-I will put it as mildly as that- to think that a man whose children are suffering from lack of food, except such as may be obtained from relief, cannot be permitted to work for a contractor unless he is endorsed and recommended by some member of parliament in this capital city, on work which is being carried on with the money of all Canada, not of one part only, and which is being maintained by the people generally.
I knew the problems of the Minister of Public Works of the recent government in that connection. I had knowledge of what perhaps hon. gentlemen have read in the newspapers, in connection with the contractor who was building the addition to the mint here. He brought to this city men from the west, and when I say the west I mean as far away as Sudbury. One of those young men came to see me, and I took the matter up with the Department of Labour. On investigation that department found that this contractor was taking ten cents an hour off the pay of this poor unfortunate. That man got his money back from the contractor, but of course that ended any possible chance he might have had of being employed there any longer, so now he is out of a job. It is unfair to say that necessitous persons must be vouched for, in connection with relief undertakings, by a political organization. As far as it was possible every effort was made by the former government to eliminate that sort of thing in the last few years.
In Quebec, I am sorry to say, in provincial undertakings in connection with roads they went so far as to put in writting a perfectly clear statement that in the particular district the vote usually had been in the proportion of, we shall say, eight to four, and they thought that those who might be recommended by the opposition to the Taschereau administration might have one-third and the other two-thirds should be recommended by the representatives of the government that was in power. And, mark you, we were contributing to that work. When the Minister of Labour raised a question about the matter, as he did, he had a good deal of difficulty. We were told that this was a

May I remind the minister that in 1914 a sum was voted for the erection of a public building at Powell River, but the construction of that building was not proceeded with because of the intervention of the war. It is now important to note the remarkable development of this important industrial community, and the fact that it has wholly inadequate facilities for the transaction of post office, customs and excise business. The buildings now in use are so inadequate that during the busy hours serious congestion occurs.
Powell River has a population of 5,400. a pay-roll now in excess of $1,125,000 annually. Goods are produced each year to the value of $7,000,000 and exported each year to the value of $4,490,000. These figures will give an idea of the amount of business transacted in the community. The registered tonnage of sea-going ships entered annually stands at 472.000 tons. I know the minister has on file a photograph of the present post office building, and I may tell him that when the men

are off shift and call for their mail the congestion and delay are serious. I made a personal inspection of the premises, and on the testimony of the local officials I may say that it is impossible efficiently to transact the business of this rapidly growing community.

It is a matter of judgment as to whether one project would provide more work than another, and would relieve unemployment in a locality to a greater extent.
These estimates are not what could really be called relief estimates. The relief assistance given by the government is given by the Department of Labour. I notice in the main estimates in connection with Richelieu river improvements, an item of $122,000. Perhaps the minister would discuss that in connection with the item before us, showing the relation, if any, between the two.
This is a revote of a contract which was awarded last year for the deepening of the Richelieu river from St. Ours to the Chambly canal.
Is one item a continuation of the other?

Yes. It is a project for developing the Richelieu river, deepening it and improving the channel. It is not a new undertaking, having been before the department for a number of years, going back as-far as 1902. In 1907 also, proposals were placed before the department for the development of the Richelieu river and the improvement of the channel for navigation in that river; and if my memory serves me, the information I obtained was that as far back as 1913 the department was practically ready to ask for tenders for the construction of a regulating dam which was to be built between the city of St. Johns and Chambly, in order to regulate the flow of the Richelieu river and at the same time to protect the low-lying lands above St. Johns, between St. Johns and the boundary line near lake Champlain. This project was not gone on with owing to the war, which broke out in 1914. The question has been before the department for a considerable time. The Richelieu river has been dredged from the St. Lawrence up to St. Ours, and the lock at St. Ours was rebuilt a number of years ago, with the same depth and the same dimensions as the locks and canals in the American territory, from lake Champlain to the Hudson river.
What is the depth?

Twelve feet. That is the depth of the New York state barge canal which runs from lake Champlain to the Hudson river. The St. Ours lock was rebuilt by the Department of Railways a few years ago at the same depth and with the same dimensions as the New York state barge canal, and in 1934 or 1935-I believe it was 1935- a contract was awarded for the deepening of the Richelieu river from St. Ours, which is being carried out to a depth of twelve feet up to Chambly, making it twelve feet from the St. Lawrence up to Chambly. What I

propose here is the building of the dam which was proposed many years ago to regulate the flow of the Richelieu river for the purpose of protecting the low-lying lands above St. Johns and at the same time to shorten the length of the Chambly canal by half. Using the river instead of the canal.

Yes, on that section. This project for the development of the Richelieu river is one which the United States have had in mind. One project which the authorities there referred to the International Joint Commission is a canal starting from lake Champlain and passing through American territory to St. Francis lake outside Montreal. What they contemplate is a canal of twenty-five or twenty-seven feet and approximately of the same depth as the proposed St. Lawrence development. That is one of their projects, and another is to 'have a similar canal started from St. Johns; that is, twenty-two miles in Canada from the boundary and running from there to somewhere near Laprairie. This would be entirely an inland canal and would be of the same depth as the first project, running through lake Champlain to lake St. Francis. The third is a project which would include the reconstruction of the Chambly canal, starting from the Chambly basin at the foot of the Chambly canal. The canal would be dug from that place up to a point near Montreal-Longueuil or Laprairie or St. Lambert. Those are the three main suggestions which the United States authorities have referred to the International Joint Commission. The fourth one is a purely Canadian project, having for its object the development of a purely Canadian watercourse.
As a matter of fact, No. 4 has been in use for years but was allowed to go into disuse.

The Chambly canal was built a long time ago, but it is not used to-day as it should be, because the depth is only five and a half or six feet. When I was a boy I used to see the Richelieu river at and above Sorel practically full of canal boats carrying all sorts of goods and materials from Quebec, Three Rivers, Montreal and even Ottawa.
